1387.title: K-R-A
1387.hook: kara: to call and to read; Mikra, scripture, is "what is called out"
1387.howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll, and members of the congregation are called up to stand beside it; Jews call the book known in English as Leviticus Vayikra, from its first word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, D-B-R: davar, a word and a thing at once, and midbar, the wilderness. Today, a new week, and a root you can hear.

An old letter from a grandmother turns up in a drawer. Nobody reads it alone. Someone unfolds it, clears their throat, and reads it out, and the room goes quiet to listen. Reading like that isn't silent. It's done with the voice, and it's aimed at somebody. Hebrew keeps that close: the verb to read and the verb to call are one verb, from one root. Kuf, resh, alef: K-R-A.
screen: `A LETTER FROM A DRAWER.` → `READ OUT TO THE ROOM.` → `K-R-A: TO CALL, TO READ.`

segments.voice: Turn kara four ways. First, calling. Leviticus opens, "And the LORD called unto Moses." The first Hebrew word is vayikra, and he called, and it became the book's Hebrew name: Vayikra. A whole book that begins with a call. Second, calling out. In Isaiah's vision, the seraphim stand above the throne, "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." Kara again: not whispered, called, so the one across can hear. Third, reading. In Nehemiah, the people gather in a square in Jerusalem. Ezra the scribe opens the book of the Torah, and all the people stand up. Then "they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." The reading is mikra. Fourth, the name. Mikra became one of the Jewish names for the Bible itself: what is called out. Not a book you take to your room, but one read aloud to people in a square, with someone beside it explaining. As you heard on day one hundred fifty-seven, synagogues still read the Torah aloud from the scroll, and people are called up to stand beside it. To call is to aim your voice at someone. To read, in Hebrew, is to do the same with a page.
screen: `VAYIKRA: AND HE CALLED.` · `ONE CALLED UNTO ANOTHER: HOLY.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK; THEY STAND.` · `MIKRA: WHAT IS CALLED OUT.` · then, large: `קָרָא`

segments.voice: On the screen is Isaiah's line, the seraphim calling to each other; read it once in your head, then out loud, slowly, as if someone across the room needs to hear it. Holy, holy, holy. Notice what changes when the words leave your mouth, the pace, the breath, the weight, and if you'd rather, read any verse you love the same way.
screen: `AND ONE CALLED UNTO ANOTHER, AND SAID:`
`HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, IS THE LORD OF HOSTS.`

segments.voice: K-R-A. Kuf, resh, alef: kara, to call and to read; mikra, scripture, what is called out. Today's word.
Your line: reading is calling. Whoever read that letter out to the room already knew it. One thousand three hundred eighty-seven days, and counting.

pairs: opened the book in the square

kara means both; K-R-A.

what a scholar hears: Nehemiah 8:8 already calls the public reading mikra, a name later used for scripture.

chat.says: Why does Hebrew use the same verb for reading and for calling?
options: Both aim your voice at someone. K-R-A covers both, and mikra means what is called out.
It doesn't; kara only means to call, and reading uses a different Hebrew root.
Because ancient Hebrew had no written books, so reading only meant shouting.
chat.meaning: Kara means to call and to read. Nehemiah's mikra, the reading, became a name for the Bible: what is called out, read aloud to people.

Vayikra.meaning: and He called: the Hebrew name of Leviticus

1388.title: S-F-R
1388.hook: sefer, sofer, sippur, mispar: book, scribe, story, number
1388.howItsDone: A Sefer Torah is written by hand by a trained sofer, a scribe; at the Passover seder, families retell the Exodus, drawing on the command to tell it to one's children, and in the weeks after Passover Jews count the days of the Omer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-R-A: to call and to read, and Ezra opening the book while the whole square stood. Today, a root that holds a whole library.

A crumpled receipt turns up in a coat pocket. A date, a time, a column of prices, a total. Read it again. Candles, flour, a birthday card, at seven on a Thursday evening. Somebody was running late for a party. The numbers are telling a story. English keeps counting and telling in separate drawers. Hebrew puts them in one root, and adds the book and the scribe. Samech, fey, resh: S-F-R.
screen: `A RECEIPT IN A COAT POCKET.` → `THE NUMBERS TELL A STORY.` → `S-F-R: COUNT, TELL, WRITE.`

segments.voice: Turn S-F-R four ways. First, sefer, a book. A Torah scroll is a Sefer Torah, a book of Torah, though it's rolled, not bound. Second, sofer, a scribe, the one who writes the book. Yesterday's Ezra, whom you first met as a sofer on day eight hundred seventy-six, is called just that: "he was a ready scribe in the Law of Moses." Ready: quick, skilled. Third, sippur, a story, from the verb to tell. Before the last plagues in Egypt, Moses is told why these things are happening: "that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son." And the Psalms: "The heavens declare the glory of God." Declare is mesaprim, they tell. The night sky, telling a story with no words at all. Fourth, mispar, a number, from the verb to count. God brings Abram outside: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." And for the weeks between Passover and Shavuot, Leviticus says, "And ye shall count unto you," day by day. Put them on one shelf. The heavens tell, and Abram is asked to count them. A father tells his son, and a scribe writes it down. In Hebrew, counting and telling are cousins. To count your days is to start telling their story, and a story told well counts what mattered.
screen: `SEFER: A BOOK.` · `SOFER: A READY SCRIBE.` · `SIPPUR: TELL IN THE EARS OF THY SON.` · `MISPAR: COUNT THE STARS.` · then, large: `סֵפֶר`

segments.voice: Count back a few days and stop on one small moment that stayed with you: something someone said, a meal, a wrong turn that went right. Tell it to yourself start to finish, the way you'd tell it at a table, and find the detail that makes it yours. Then think of one person who'd like to hear it, and if you pray, hold the moment in the quiet.
S-F-R. Samech, fey, resh: sefer, a book; sofer, a scribe; sippur, a story; mispar, a number. Counting and telling in one root. Today's word.
Your line: books, stories, numbers. The receipt in the coat pocket knew it all along. Rest well.

myth: in Hebrew, to count and to tell come from the same root
mispar, number, and sippur, story, both come from S-F-R.
Psalm 19 says the heavens keep silent about God
"The heavens declare the glory of God": mesaprim, they tell.
a Torah scroll is not called a book because it's rolled
it's a Sefer Torah, a book of Torah, rolled or not.

options: name every star.
count the stars, if he can.
go back inside and sleep.
fork.reveal: "count the stars, if thou be able to count them." then: so shall thy seed be.

original.note: Hebrew: a book; from S-F-R, the root of counting and telling.

trapdoor: what you thought: numbers and stories have nothing to do with each other.
what it means: in Hebrew, sefer, sofer, sippur and mispar all grow from S-F-R.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 19's heavens mesaprim, they tell, while Abram is told lispor, to count, the stars.
guess: a root for counting and telling, and so books and scribes
a root for writing on stone, used for the commandments
a root for the shofar, the horn blown on the holidays

chat.says: What do a book, a scribe, a story and a number have in common in Hebrew?
options: One root, S-F-R: in Hebrew, counting and telling are cousins.
They're unrelated words grouped in one Bible verse by chance.
They all come from shofar, the horn blown on the holidays.
chat.meaning: Sefer, sofer, sippur and mispar all come from S-F-R. The heavens tell, Abram counts the stars: counting and telling in one root.

sefer.meaning: Hebrew: a book, even a rolled scroll

sofer.meaning: Hebrew: a scribe, who writes the book

sippur.meaning: Hebrew: a story, from the verb to tell

mispar.meaning: Hebrew: a number, from the verb to count

Shavuot.meaning: the festival seven weeks after Passover

1389.title: Y-R-H
1389.hook: Torah is linked to yarah: to aim, to point, to teach
1389.howItsDone: Jews read the Torah aloud in synagogue and study it with commentaries; in Hebrew a teacher is a moreh, from the root that tradition links to the word Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, S-F-R: sefer, sofer, sippur, mispar, the receipt that turned out to be a story. Today, the root tradition hears inside the word Torah.

A stranger on the sidewalk, phone dead, clearly lost, asks how to get to the train. Nobody hands over a rulebook. You lift an arm and point. That way, past the bakery, then left. The whole answer is in the arm: a direction, aimed. Hold that picture next to a word often translated as law. Torah. Jewish tradition links it to a root that has nothing to do with courtrooms. Yud, resh, heh: Y-R-H. Yarah. To shoot. To point. To teach.
screen: `A LOST STRANGER.` → `AN ARM THAT POINTS.` → `Y-R-H: SHOOT, POINT, TEACH.`

segments.voice: Turn yarah four ways. First, shooting. Jonathan, King Saul's son, needs to warn his friend David without being seen. He goes out to a field with a boy and a bow: "Run, find now the arrows which I shoot." Where the arrows land is the message. Shoot is from this root; an arrow is aim made visible. Second, pointing the way. When Jacob's family goes down to Egypt, Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph "to show the way before him unto Goshen." To show the way, l'horot, again Y-R-H. Not carrying anyone. Pointing. Third, teaching. A teacher is a moreh, the one who points. In Proverbs a parent says, "Hear, my son, the instruction of thy father, And forsake not the teaching of thy mother." The teaching of thy mother: torat imecha, a phrase you met on day one thousand forty-two. The old Jewish Publication Society translation renders torah there not as law, but as teaching. Fourth, the Torah itself. English often calls it the Law, and it does contain law. But, as you first heard on day twenty, tradition hears this root underneath: a teaching that aims you and sends you out, like Jonathan's arrow or Judah on the road to Goshen. Not a fence around you. An arm lifted, saying: that way. Open a Torah scroll, by this reading, and you're asking for directions.
screen: `SHOOT: JONATHAN'S ARROWS.` · `POINT: JUDAH SHOWS THE WAY.` · `TEACH: THE TEACHING OF THY MOTHER.` · `TORAH: A TEACHING THAT AIMS YOU.` · then, large: `תּוֹרָה`

segments.voice: Let the week ahead come into view and pick one thing worth aiming at, small and real: finish a letter, visit someone, learn one more line. Picture it as a target a little way off, and then the arrow leaving the bow, the very first step you'd take toward it. Hold your aim steady, and if you pray, bring the goal into the quiet.
Y-R-H. Yud, resh, heh: yarah, to shoot, to point, to teach; moreh, a teacher; and, tradition says, Torah, a teaching that aims. Today's word.
Your line: torah means aiming. A mother's torah is the way she points her child. I'll be here tomorrow.

pairs: run, find the arrows I shoot

Proverbs uses it for a mother's teaching: forsake not the teaching of thy mother.
the root Y-R-H can mean to shoot an arrow

Yes; the word comes from a root for courts and judges, and nothing else.
No, Torah means scroll; it names the parchment, not what's written on it.

1390.title: Ch-T-A
1390.hook: chet, sin, means missing the mark, as slingers "not missing" (Judges 20:16)
1390.howItsDone: In the Yom Kippur liturgy Jews recite the Al Chet, a confession whose lines begin "for the sin," al chet, said together as a community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-R-H: yarah, to shoot and to point, Jonathan's arrows and Judah showing the way. Today, what happens when the arrow goes wide.

Last seconds of a high-school game. A kid steps to the free-throw line, bounces the ball, breathes, shoots. It clangs off the front of the rim. The gym goes quiet. Nobody calls it evil. Nobody says the kid is a bad person. It's a miss, and the coach will say: bend your knees, follow through, again. Hold onto that gym. A Hebrew word for sin comes from a verb the Bible uses for exactly this. Chet, tet, alef: Ch-T-A. To miss.
screen: `OFF THE FRONT OF THE RIM.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT EVIL.` → `CH-T-A: TO MISS.`

segments.voice: Turn Ch-T-A four ways. First, the slingers. Judges describes left-handed fighters from the tribe of Benjamin who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. Not miss is lo yachati, from this very root. Before it's a moral word, it's a stone flying wide. Second, the noun. Chet is one of the Bible's words for sin, and you can hear the slingers inside it: an aim that went off, a target that was there, a stone that didn't reach it. Third, nobody is perfect. Ecclesiastes says it flatly: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." The verse doesn't say the target is fake, or that aim doesn't matter. It says everyone who shoots will sometimes miss. Fourth, why we miss. Proverbs adds what anyone who's been late knows: the one who hurries with his feet misses, again Ch-T-A. Speed, carelessness, a stone thrown without looking. Put it beside yesterday. If Torah is aiming, chet is the miss, and both belong to the same practice. A miss is serious; someone can get hurt by a stone that goes wide. But a miss can also be studied. Where did it go? Was I rushing? What would I adjust? The coach at the free-throw line is already asking this root's question.
screen: `SLINGERS WHO DID NOT MISS.` · `CHET: A STONE THAT FLIES WIDE.` · `NOT A RIGHTEOUS MAN WHO SINNETH NOT.` · `HURRYING FEET MISS.` · then, large: `חֵטְא`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small miss from the past few days, a sharp word, a promise that slipped, a moment you rushed past someone, and look at where the stone landed without arguing with it or punishing yourself. Then ask the coach's questions: was I hurrying, what was I really aiming at, what one adjustment would bring the next shot closer? Hold that adjustment, and if you pray, bring the miss into the quiet.
Ch-T-A. Chet, tet, alef: the root of chet, sin, from a verb for missing the mark, like a slinger's stone that goes wide. Today's word.
Your line: sin is missing the mark. Even the good miss. See you at the next one.

pairs: not a righteous man who sinneth not

No, chet comes from a root for darkness, like a stain on the soul.
Yes, but only in modern Hebrew slang; the Bible never uses it that way.

1391.title: K-P-R
1391.hook: kaparah, Yom Kippur: to cover over, to wipe clean
1391.howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged to ask forgiveness, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day atones for wrongs between people only once the wronged person has been appeased; the day itself is kept with fasting and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-T-A: chet, the stone that flies wide, the free throw off the rim. Today, what comes after the miss.

"Make thee an ark of gopher wood." Noah gets his instructions: the wood, the rooms, the measurements. And one step that's easy to skip past. Before the rain, before the animals, every seam has to be smeared with thick, dark pitch, inside and out, so the water can't get in. Sticky, unglamorous work. Without it, the ark is a very large box that sinks. Keep that pot of pitch in view. Its Hebrew name shares three letters with a holy day. Kaf, fey, resh: K-P-R.
screen: `MAKE THEE AN ARK.` → `SEAL EVERY SEAM WITH PITCH.` → `K-P-R: COVER.`

segments.voice: Turn K-P-R four ways. First, the pitch. Noah "shalt pitch it within and without with pitch." To pitch and the pitch both come from this root: kofer, a coating that covers. Second, the cover. The ark of the covenant, the box that holds the tablets, gets a lid of pure gold called the kapporet, the ark-cover. On it, the text says, God will meet with Moses. A covering, and a holy one. Third, the day. Yom Kippur, the day of atonements. Leviticus: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." Hear both pictures: covering over, like pitch on a seam, and wiping clean. Fourth, the catch, which you met on day six hundred fifty-two. The Mishnah, near the end of tractate Yoma, says: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between one person and another, it does not, until the wrongdoer makes peace with the person they hurt. The day can't do that part for you. So before the fast, some people call each other, or knock on doors: I'm sorry for what I said in the spring. Atonement covers. But like Noah's pitch, it doesn't spread itself. Someone has to pick up the brush and work it into the seam, one gap at a time.
screen: `KOFER: PITCH, INSIDE AND OUT.` · `KAPPORET: THE GOLDEN ARK-COVER.` · `YOM KIPPUR: COVERED, CLEANSED.` · `BETWEEN PEOPLE: GO TO THEM FIRST.` · then, large: `כַּפָּרָה`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small wrong you did that still has a gap in it, a word that stung, a call you didn't return, a favor you let drop, and picture the person. Then picture one good thing that could cover that seam: an apology, plain and specific, a call, the favor done late. Choose it, and if you pray, bring that person into the quiet.
K-P-R. Kaf, fey, resh: kofer, the pitch on Noah's ark; kapporet, the ark-cover; kaparah, atonement, as in Yom Kippur. To cover over, to wipe clean. Today's word.
Your line: atonement covers. Between people, the covering starts with the person you hurt. Go gently.

1392.title: S-L-Ch
1392.howItsDone: Jews ask for pardon in a blessing of the weekday Amidah, and in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur many communities gather, often late at night, to say penitential prayers called Selichot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-P-R: kaparah, the covering that gives Yom Kippur its name. Today, the word that comes next.

Someone bumps your cart in the grocery aisle and says, "Sorry, excuse me." In Israel, in that same aisle, the word is slicha. It's everyday Hebrew for excuse me, and for I'm sorry, said over and over before lunch without a thought. Then, in the season before the High Holy Days, the same root fills synagogues, often late at night or before dawn, for prayers called Selichot. Pardons. The word you use to get past someone's cart is the word people use to stand before God. Samekh, lamed, chet: S-L-Ch.
screen: `SLICHA: EXCUSE ME.` → `SELICHOT: NIGHT PRAYERS.` → `S-L-CH: TO PARDON.`

segments.voice: S-L-Ch gives salach, to pardon, and selichah, pardon or forgiveness. Turn it four ways. First, a plea in the wilderness. In Numbers, the people lose heart and want to turn back to Egypt, and Moses pleads for them. The answer comes in two Hebrew words, salachti kidvarecha. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have pardoned according to thy word." Pardon doesn't erase what happened. The story goes on, with consequences. But the relationship holds. Second, Psalm one hundred thirty, out of the depths: "For with Thee there is forgiveness, that Thou mayest be feared." Some readers find that surprising; you might expect forgiveness to make people careless. The psalm ties it to awe instead. Third, the prayer book. In the weekday Amidah, the standing prayer, one blessing asks plainly for pardon, the blessing you met on day five hundred eighty-three. Forgiveness isn't saved for one holy day. It's part of an ordinary Tuesday. Fourth, the grocery aisle again. Some readers notice that in the Bible this verb is used of God's pardon, while modern Hebrew spends it on small bumps between people. The root holds both: the large pardon you can't earn, and the small one you hand a stranger all day long.
screen: `A PLEA: I HAVE PARDONED.` · `A PSALM: WITH THEE IS FORGIVENESS.` · `A PRAYER: PARDON, EVERY WEEKDAY.` · `AN AISLE: SLICHA, EXCUSE ME.` · then, large: `סְלִיחָה`

segments.voice: Let a small irritation come to mind, nothing heavy: a text left unanswered, a dish left in the sink, a driver who cut in, and notice where you're still holding it, in the jaw, the shoulders, the story you keep telling. Then quietly let the small thing be pardoned, not because it was fine, but because it's small and you'd like your hands back. If you pray, you can bring the person's name with you into the quiet.
S-L-Ch. Samekh, lamed, chet: the root of salach, to pardon, and selichah, forgiveness, which is also how Hebrew says excuse me. Today's word.
Your line: forgive. Even excuse me has a pardon underneath it. That's today, done.

pairs: prayers before the High Holy Days
excuse me, in the grocery aisle

1393.title: M-Ch-L
1393.howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged and ask for mechilah, forgiveness, and traditional prayer books include a declaration of forgiveness for others at the start of the bedtime Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, S-L-Ch: selichah, pardon, and slicha, excuse me. Today, the word for letting a debt go.

A friend borrowed some cash in the spring. It's autumn now. Neither of you mentions it, and both of you remember it every time you split a check. There are three ways this ends. Somebody pays. Somebody nags. Or the lender says, out loud, forget it, we're square, and means it. That third ending has a name in the language of the rabbis: mechilah. It's the word for waiving a claim, and the word Jews use, especially before Yom Kippur, when they ask one another for forgiveness. Mem, chet, lamed: M-Ch-L.
screen: `A DEBT NOBODY MENTIONS.` → `PAY, NAG, OR WAIVE.` → `M-CH-L: TO WAIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's root was pardon. Today's is quieter and more practical: mechilah is giving up something you're owed. Turn it four ways. First, the ledger. In the rabbis' legal language, if someone owes you and you say machul lach, it's waived, the debt is gone. Nobody pays it back. You simply stop holding the paper. Second, the question. Two days ago came the Mishnah's line: between people, Yom Kippur waits until they make peace. Mechilah is what one person asks the other in that moment. Not, do you feel better? Not, was it fine? Will you waive it? Third, the asker's side. The Talmud discusses the person you hurt who won't grant it, and teaches that you keep trying, sincerely and with others present, but there is a limit. Asking for forgiveness is a duty. Forcing it is not. Fourth, the night. In traditional prayer books, the bedtime Shema, which you met on day one hundred twenty, opens with a short paragraph forgiving anyone who wronged you, in word or in deed. Every night, a small mechilah before sleep. Look back at this week: calling out, books, aiming, missing the mark, covering, pardon, and now waiving. One long walk from what's written to what's owed.
screen: `THE LEDGER: MACHUL, IT'S WAIVED.` · `THE QUESTION: WILL YOU WAIVE IT?` · `THE ASKER: ASK, DON'T FORCE.` · `THE NIGHT: FORGIVEN BEFORE SLEEP.` · then, large: `מְחִילָה`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something small someone owes you, money, an apology, a returned favor, a call they never made, and if what comes up is a deep hurt, choose something smaller for today. Notice how long you've carried it, then try the bedtime words silently in your own voice: whatever this person owes me, I let it go. You don't have to tell them or pretend it was fine; just put the paper down, and if you pray, bring their name into the quiet.
M-Ch-L. Mem, chet, lamed: the root of mechilah, waiving what you're owed, and the forgiveness Jews ask of one another before Yom Kippur. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. Waiving a debt isn't pretending it was fine. Sleep well tonight.
